n: Hearing his father was ill, Joseph brought his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, so they could receive Jacob’s blessing.
Told that Joseph was coming, Israel gathered his strength and sat up—preparing for a sacred moment.
Jacob recalls how God Almighty appeared to him at Luz (Bethel) and blessed him. He passes on the covenant by first remembering it.
Jacob repeats the promise: many descendants and the land of Canaan forever. These are the core blessings of the Abrahamic covenant.
Jacob adopts Ephraim and Manasseh as his own sons, equal to Reuben and Simeon. Each will become a full tribe, giving Joseph a double portion—the birthright share.
Any later children of Joseph would be counted under Ephraim and Manasseh for inheritance. The Joseph Smith Translation adds several verses here about Joseph’s descendants being preserved.

f.g: JST Genesis 48:7-11 expands this with a prophecy about Joseph’s seed.

n: Jacob remembers Rachel, who died near Bethlehem on the journey home. Adopting Rachel’s grandsons may be partly his way of honoring her.

f.g: an older name for the Bethlehem area

n: Nearly blind, Israel notices the young men and asks who they are—a formal question that begins the blessing ritual.
Joseph answers that God has given him these sons in Egypt. Jacob asks for them so he can bless them.
Like his father Isaac before him, Jacob was nearly blind with age. He kissed and embraced the boys.

f.w: the eyes of Israel were dim

n: Jacob marvels: he never expected to see Joseph again, and now God has let him see Joseph’s children too.
Joseph took the boys from Jacob’s knees—a sign of adoption—and bowed deeply in respect.

f.g: Placing children on the knees was a gesture of adoption.

n: Joseph carefully positioned Manasseh, the older, at Jacob’s right hand (the hand of greater blessing) and Ephraim at his left.

f.g: the hand symbolizing priority and strength

n: But Jacob crossed his arms deliberately, placing his right hand on Ephraim, the younger. Once again in Genesis, the younger is chosen over the older.

f.g: Laying on of hands is an ancient pattern for priesthood blessing.

n: Jacob blesses Joseph through his sons, describing God as the One his fathers walked with and who “shepherded” him all his life.
Jacob calls on “the Angel which redeemed me”—the divine messenger he wrestled with and saw. He asks that his covenant name and his fathers’ rest on these boys and that they grow into multitudes.

f.w: let my name be named on them
f.g: let them carry on my covenant identity

n: Joseph was unhappy and tried to move his father’s right hand to Manasseh’s head.
Joseph corrects his father: “This is the firstborn.”
Jacob refuses: “I know it, my son.” He acted by inspiration, not by mistake. Both would be great, but Ephraim’s descendants would become “a multitude of nations.”

f.g: Latter-day Saints see this fulfilled in part in Ephraim’s role in the latter-day gathering.

n: Jacob made the boys a model for future blessings: Israelites would say, “God make thee as Ephraim and as Manasseh.” Jewish fathers still bless their sons with these words.
Jacob assures Joseph that even after his death God will bring the family back to the promised land.

f.w: bring you again unto the land of your fathers

n: Jacob gives Joseph an extra portion of land. The Hebrew word for “portion” is shechem—a pun on the city of Shechem, where Joseph was later buried.

f.g: Hebrew shekem, “shoulder” or “ridge,” likely a play on Shechem
